“One more time” written by John Carr and Ken Mott 1992 Lake Charles,La.
videos.description:
A song Ken Mott and i wrote in 1992 at a point in time when we were both recently dumped by our girlfriends. 

At that time we were jammin with Parnell and Sean Babineaux. 
Parnell had a reel to reel 4 track recorder. We recorded a version of this with a few acoustic guitars, bass and a piano at “high res=double the tape speed” on said 4 track. 
We then backup/ saved the recording to standard cassette. 

Years later i found the cassette. Threw it in my tascam 4 track player and remembered the high res recording. 
The cassette made it sound being played at 50% speed. 

By now pc’s were around. I sped it up in the computer, and now being a more proficient guitar player i learned the solo Ken played note for note. 

I would still love to record a full band version of this song with harmonies n all but i wouldnt dare do it without Ken at my side.  To this day, i still think its a fantastic tune!!!

Love ya forever, Ken!
Cheers to the good ole days, bud!

videos.title: 80's Rock-Riff Harmony
videos.description:
http://www.andrewwasson.com/

Andrew Wasson of Creative Guitar Studio answers questions from off of his Guitar Blog website...

Q). I'd classify myself as an intermediate guitarist, learning how to play 80's power-chord rock. I like that sound of classic rock bands from the 1980's a lot. But, bands like; Ratt, Tesla and Quiet Riot, seem to have other chords in their songs. These are a lot like power-chords, but yet different. It's like they use major & minor chords but with an open, "ringing" sound. How do they do this?
Raymond -- Highland, Indiana, USA

A). Bands from the 1980's were chock full of great guitar players. Guys like George Lynch from Dokken and Warren Demartini from Ratt, could not only shred the neck to pieces, but they were also killer rhythm players, embellishing all kinds of interesting two-note chord concepts around those common power-chord shapes! Now, the shapes that were most often used were small major, or minor two-note chords, and they were simply mixed in with the use of the standard power-chords. The final end result was a progression that slurred the punchy power-chord concept along with the more harmonic double-stop majors & minors. This gave 80's Rock progressions a very interesting scalar sound that allowed for rapid harmony movement along the neck. In the video I zoom in on the fret-board and apply some of these classic 80's rock guitar harmony ideas. Enjoy!
